newsitem.title: USA: Georgian diplomat charged in auto accident case.
newsitem.headline: Georgian diplomat charged in auto accident case.

text.p: A Georgian diplomat, stripped of diplomatic immunity, surrendered to police and was charged on Thursday with causing a car accident that killed a teenage girl and injured four others, U.S. prosecutors said.

U.S. Attorney Eric Holder told a news conference Gueorgui Makharadze, his country's No. 2 diplomat in Washington, turned himself in after the Republic of Georgia took the rare step over the weekend of waiving his diplomatic immunity.

Makharadze, 35, was taken into custody and charged with involuntary manslaughter in connection of the January 4 death of Joviane Waltrick, a 16-year-old Brazilian girl living in the Washington suburb of Kensington, Maryland.

He also was charged with four counts of aggravated assault involving the others who were injured in the five-car crash in downtown Washington. The charges carry a maximum punishment of 70 years in prison.

Holder said blood tests taken two hours after the accident at a hospital showed Makharadze had an alcohol level almost twice the legal limit. Witnesses said he had been driving as fast as 80 miles per hour (129 kph), right before the crash.

In an affidavit with the arrest warrant, police detective Michael Harvey said Makharadze "operated his vehicle while intoxicated at a grossly excessive speed and in a reckless manner in an area congested with pedestrians and traffic."
He said several witnesses testified that Makharadze, right before the crash, was among a party of three that had dinner at a restaurant, and that they drank three carafes of wine.
Harvey said the witnesses said that Makharadze also had several other glasses of wine and a shot of liqueur.

Harvey recounted witness testimony that Makharadze lost control of his car and ran into a vehicle waiting at a stop light. The force of the crash catapulted the second vehicle into a third car, killing Waltrick, who was a passenger in it.

The day after the accident, Makharadze said during a police interview that he drank only two glasses of wine and that the regular and emergency brakes on his 1997 model Ford Taurus car had failed. He said the gas pedal had stuck.
But Harvey said a city mechanic and two outside experts inspected the car after the crash and concluded the brakes and the accelerator pedal had not failed.

Prosecutor Holder said Makharadze was processed by the police, a step that includes having his fingerprints and his photograph taken. An arraignment had been set for late Thursday afternoon in a local court.
Holder said prosecutors wanted Makharadze to surrender his passport but he probably would be freed on certain conditions, possibly to the custody of a third party, such as the embassy.
Holder would not rule out a possible plea deal later, but emphasised that on the most serious manslaughter charge Makharadze would have to admit guilt.

Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze said this week, after waiving diplomatic immunity, that he may seek to have Makharadze serve any prison time in Georgia, rather than the United States, if he is convicted.
Holder praised Shevardnadze for a "courageous and principled decision." He added that Georgia's "actions have ensured that justice will be done in this matter."
Makharadze was a rising star in the Georgian foreign service, making the decision to grant the waiver of immunity an even harder one for Shevardnadze.
Holder said a grand jury next will indict Makharadze on the same charges as contained in the arrest warrant.
